item.title: How To Use Decision Models for Evals
item.abstract: Decision models have exploded onto the scene recently, starting with TypeSafe’s Jev, followed by Perplexity’s Decider, Liquid’s d1, Cloudflare’s Clef, and OpenAI’s Decisions API 1 . These models promise fast, inexpensive classification. Decision models are an appealing low-cost alternative to LLM judges 2 for automated evals. But whether they’re the right choice depends on the cost, performance, and latency requirements of your use case. We’ve also noticed people using the default decision threshold of 0.50 without checking whether it works well for their task. This can leave a lot of performance on the table. In this post, we’ll start by showing how to tune thresholds to get the best results from decision models. With those thresholds tuned, we’ll compare cost and performance to help you assess which model fits your use case. Finally, we’ll explore how to interpret model scores when deciding whether to act, and how calibration can make them more useful as confidence estimates. We used 100 traces, or logs of conversations and actions, from an apartment leasing agent. The task is to identify traces containing an error, such as a failed booking or a missed handoff to a human. 3 We used the same dataset and broad failure-finding task in our prior post on automated evals . Here, each decision model returns a failure probability for each trace. We tested Jev 1.13, Perplexity Decider 1.1 27B, Liquid d1 and d1-ultra, Cloudflare Clef Flash, and OpenAI Decisions (GPT-6 Luna) 1 . Each model received the same evaluation criteria. The appendix shows the prompt and the structured version used for Jev. We compare models on two dimensions: For brevity, we leave latency aside because it depends on factors outside this experiment’s control. 5 We assign each trace one of two labels, pass or fail. This is a binary pass/fail eval , which we recommend because it encourages clear criteria and is easier to align with human preferences. Each decision model returns a score from 0 to 1 that estimates how likely a trace is to contain a failure. The APIs turn this score into a decision using a default decision threshold of 0.50 . Traces with scores at or above the threshold are flagged as failures. Using this default without checking it against your data can give you subpar results. For example, a model could assign every failure a score of 0.40 and every passing trace a score of 0.10. Even though this model classifies traces perfectly at a threshold of 0.30, the default threshold of 0.50 would catch nothing. In practice, scores for failures and passing traces will overlap. Lowering the threshold catches more failures but can also raise more false alarms. Choosing a threshold means balancing: The right tradeoff depends on your business goals. For example, criminal trials set a high bar for conviction to avoid convicting innocent people, emphasizing precision. Cancer screening may emphasize recall, accepting more false alarms to miss fewer cases. 6 For this comparison, we’ll give precision and recall equal weight using the F1 score , their harmonic mean. F1 ranges from 0 to 1, and higher is better. The curves below show how each model scores failures (orange) and passing traces (blue). Taller parts of a curve mean more scores from that class fall in that range. Scores at or above the dashed threshold line are flagged. Use the toggle to compare 0.50 with Optimized for best F1 , which chooses a threshold for each model. 7 OpenAI separates the two classes best on this task, which is also reflected in its higher F1 score. It’s also important not to blindly maximize F1 without thinking about your minimum requirements for the classifier to be useful. For example, if this classifier is used for an automated alerting system, I would want a minimum of 80% on both precision and recall so that I’m minimizing false alarms while catching a sufficient number of failures. The chart below shows how precision and recall change at different thresholds. 8 The shaded region marks where both reach at least 80%. Perplexity, Liquid d1-ultra, and OpenAI Decisions meet our requirements, but we still need to choose a decision threshold within the shaded region for each model. In the next section, we’ll discuss how to tune those thresholds. For this example, we’ll optimize F1. For our candidates, we’ll restrict tuning to thresholds that meet both 80% minimums on the training data whenever possible. We leave the other models unconstrained to illustrate the effect of tuning. 9 With labeled traces and saved model scores, you can ask a coding agent to tune the thresholds. Below is an example prompt you can modify for your use case: Using my saved model scores and binary labels (1 means failure), tune a decision threshold to maximize F1 while requiring at least 80% precision and 80% recall. Use stratified five-fold cross-validation, choosing thresholds on the training examples and measuring performance on the remaining examples. If comparing models, use the same splits for each. Only select thresholds that meet both minimums on the training examples. If none qualifies, report that rather than relaxing either requirement. Report validation precision, recall, and F1, along with any splits where no threshold qualified or validation performance fell below my minimums. Compare with the default threshold of 0.50. Reuse the saved scores without making new model calls. Here’s how tuning for F1 changed each model’s performance. We group the three candidates from the precision-recall chart together and show the other models in gray to illustrate how much tuning can help. Our candidate models gained less from F1 tuning than Liquid d1 and Clef Flash, which fell below our minimums. However, even a small shift in precision and recall can affect business costs or the user experience, so choose the tradeoff deliberately. In practice, it’s unlikely that precision and recall are equally important (as we assumed in this post with F1). For example, the F-beta score lets you give precision more weight with beta below 1, or recall more weight with beta above 1. Optimizing a different metric could lead to different thresholds and results. The chart below compares each model’s F1 (after tuning) against cost, focused on our remaining candidates: The dashed line shows the Pareto frontier among our remaining candidates. For any given F1 score, it identifies the cheapest candidate that meets or exceeds that score. This particular chart is a bit silly as there are only three options, but it’s a useful illustration for how to think about cost vs. performance. Perplexity was the cheapest of these candidates at 0.82 cents per 100 eval runs, with an F1 of 0.79. OpenAI Decisions reached an F1 of 0.87 at 3.72 cents per 100 eval runs, about 4.5 times the cost. Beyond pass/fail evals, you may want to use a decision model’s score as a confidence estimate. But can you take that number literally? For a score of 0.80 to mean an 80% chance of failure, roughly 80% of traces with similar scores should contain failures. The chart below shows each model’s probability calibration : how closely its predicted probabilities match observed outcomes. 10 Each point represents about 20 traces with similar scores. A point on the diagonal means the predicted probability matches the failure rate in that group. Above the line, the model underestimates the risk of failure. Below it, the model overestimates that risk. If the predicted probabilities don’t match the observed outcomes, we can adjust them using another model. The second panel shows one method, Platt scaling , which fits a simple curve to make that adjustment. 11 Perplexity, Liquid d1, and Clef Flash move closer to the diagonal after calibration. For example, one group of Clef Flash traces had an average predicted failure probability of about 8%, but 60% contained failures. Jev and Liquid d1-ultra were already well calibrated on this dataset and needed little adjustment.

item.title: NVIDIA Cosmos3-H-Dreams: Bringing Clinical Surgery to Life Through Generative Simulation
item.abstract: Back to Articles NVIDIA Cosmos3-H-Dreams: Bringing Clinical Surgery to Life Through Generative Simulation Enterprise + Article Published October 20, 2026 Upvote - Lukas Zbinden lzbinden Follow nvidia Javier Gamazo javirk1 Follow nvidia Nigel Nelson nigeln Follow nvidia Mostafa Toloui mtoloui Follow nvidia Sean Huver shuver Follow nvidia Picture moving the Cadiere grasper, grasping the gallbladder, and lifting it, all within a generated surgical scene that responds in real time. Today, we take the next step and introduce Cosmos3-H-Dreams, bringing interactive generative simulation to the visual and procedural complexity of clinical surgery with our most convincing in-body imagery to date. Our first Cosmos-H-Dreams release, built on Cosmos-Predict2.5, brought interactive generative simulation to dVRK tabletop suturing, a foundational proving ground for surgical robotics. As world foundation model (WFM), Cosmos-H-Dreams demonstrated an alternative to numerical simulation: rather than explicitly modeling scene geometry, tissue deformation, and physical interactions, it learned visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics, yielding interactive tabletop task simulation with high realism. Today, Cosmos3-H-Dreams advances this capability by learning from video and robot kinematics recording during clinical procedures on the CMR Surgical Versius platform. To our knowledge, this is the first real-time generative surgical simulator trained on clinical cholecystectomy recordings to support live kinematic control. Powered by Cosmos 3 and accelerated with FlashDreams, NVIDIA’s accelerated streaming-inference library, Cosmos3-H-Dreams runs interactively on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU. 1. From Tabletop Tasks to Clinical Scenes In a controlled tabletop environment like that of Cosmos-H-Dreams, instruments operate against a relatively simple background. Inside the human body, however, small instrument movements can affect an entire scene: tissue stretches under traction, reflections shift, structures become occluded, and smoke changes visibility. Given an initial image and supplied tool actions, a generative simulator must capture these responses while preserving the anatomy and instruments as it generates each new block of video. Small errors can accumulate over time, gradually changing instrument geometry or anatomical structure, making temporal consistency essential. Visual realism is therefore a starting point for validation, not proof of biomechanical accuracy. The generated scene must also follow the controls: translation, rotation, and gripper commands should produce coherent anatomical consequences. A plausible-looking rollout that ignores those commands cannot serve as an interactive environment. Maintaining this fidelity and responsiveness in a live control loop requires low latency generation. Cosmos3-H-Dreams addresses this setting through a model specialized for clinical cholecystectomy and distilled for real-time generation, bringing action-conditioned interaction into scenes with complex anatomy, tissue motion, and occlusion. 2. What is New in Cosmos3-H-Dreams? 2.1 A Cosmos 3 Foundation and Richer Surgical Controls Cosmos3-H-Dreams builds on Cosmos3-H-Embodied-Nano , a 16-billion-parameter model pretrained on Open-H-Embodiment , and specializes a bidirectional teacher on curated cholecystectomy video and kinematics. Sample selection targets two visible, engaged instruments, a left Cadiere grasper and a right monopolar hook, and limits camera commands to emphasize instrument-driven interaction. The model uses 28 action dimensions: pose and gripper information for both arms, plus energy controls, thumbstick axes and thumbstick buttons. Training uses 832 x 480 video with actions aligned at 10 Hz; that sampling rate is distinct from runtime generation throughput. 2.2 From Teacher to Four-Step and Two-Step Students Cosmos3-H-Dreams combines a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long autoregressive rollouts with accelerated streaming inference through FlashDreams. We first adapt the bidirectional teacher on 24 future frames, then extend the horizon to 72 frames, 2.4 and 7.2 seconds at 10 Hz. This gives the teacher longer sequences over which to learn surgical dynamics. Next, distillation turns the bidirectional teacher into a causal student that can generate video in short blocks as new actions arrive. Causal teacher forcing prepares the student for sequential generation using recorded context. Self-Forcing then trains it on its own generated context, guided by the teacher and a learned critic. This helps address the accumulation of errors during interactive rollouts. The first released student uses four denoising steps per generated block. We then train that student further with a two-step schedule to produce the second release checkpoint. The two-step model is separately trained, not simply the four-step model run with fewer sampling steps. Fewer denoising steps results in faster inference time at the expense of lower visual quality. Both checkpoints let developers explore the balance between visual quality and inference cost. 2.3 Streaming through FlashDreams FlashDreams supplies the accelerated streaming runtime. Long rollouts also require managing the model’s attention history. The Cosmos3-H-Dreams integration uses an adapted FadeMem module that consolidates the growing key/value cache during long rollouts. This complements Self-Forcing: distillation addresses how the model learns from its generated history, while cache consolidation addresses how that history is stored during streaming generation. 3. Exploring Unseen Trajectories During a clinical procedure there may be complications or some room for the surgeon to perform “novel” movements. Therefore, a simulator must be able to generalize beyond the training data, and produce coherent frames with unseen movements. The demonstrations below show Cosmos3-H-Dreams generating different cholecystectomy scenes conditioned on instrument actions recorded with a VR headset. The two videos begin with the same initial frame but follow different action sequences illustrating how instrument control leads to distinct continuations of the same scene with physically accurate tissue deformations. Furthermore, these rollouts allow us to inspect whether instruments follow the controls, whether tissue responds coherently to interaction, and whether anatomical and instrument appearance remain consistent over time. 4. Adapting to Your Own Data and Controller Cosmos3-H-Dreams includes four-step and two-step checkpoints for cholecystectomy. The system can be adapted to other datasets and embodiments with synchronized video and compatible action representations. To train a real-time student model on your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and Self-Forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide . It describes data preparation, public teacher-training tools, and the distillation stages. Controller integrations must use the same action conventions and normalization as training. 5. What is Next The advance in visual realism opens several research directions: Model the full procedure. Expand coverage and temporal consistency so all phases of cholecystectomy can be explored systematically, with clear task boundaries and success criteria. Connect generative and numerical simulation. Combine learned visual realism with explicit geometry, contact and tissue mechanics. Numerical models and measured data could help constrain and validate deformation, making simulation behavior inspectable as well as convincing. Evaluate with surgeons. Assess anatomical accuracy, instrument behavior and tissue response, turning expert feedback into reproducible benchmarks. Support more instruments. Move beyond two controlled tools to richer coordination, occlusion and interaction. Develop autonomous surgical policies.

item.title: Google has joined Amazon in attacking Nvidia’s stronghold with AI app developers
item.abstract: On Tuesday, Google announced that TorchTPU, its long-awaited version of PyTorch, is now available as an open-source project. With this, Google joins Amazon in trying to break Nvidia’s stranglehold on the AI industry, where most AI apps are written by default to run on Nvidia’s chips, or GPUs. PyTorch is the popular open-source toolkit that AI app developers and startups use to build, train, and run AI models. It is, by some accounts, used by 85% of the AI apps. PyTorch was originally developed by Meta (then Facebook) in 2016, long before the world had an inkling that LLMs would change the world. At the time, Nvidia’s GPUs were already the standard hardware for AI research, so many of PyTorch’s features were built to work specifically with them. In 2022, Meta turned PyTorch over to the Linux Foundation, a nonprofit that manages many important open source projects. Google’s version, TorchTPU, lets AI apps run on Google’s AI chips, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also makes it easy to move existing PyTorch apps to TPUs and, therefore, to Google Cloud. Developers can do this with a simple configuration change and no re-writing of their apps. Amazon made a similar announcement Monday, when it released its own version of PyTorch, called TorchNeuron. TorchNeuron allows AI apps to be ported to Amazon’s homegrown AI chip, Trainium, and to AWS with no rewriting. Amazon also said it going even further in its effort to loosen Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch. It is submitting code to the main PyTorch project that decouples various features from Nvidia’s chips, making it more open to any hardware by default. Google may be one-upping Amazon in a few ways, however. It says it worked directly with Meta, Hugging Face, Inferact (maker of vLLM) RadixArk (maker of SGLang), and others to ensure that TorchTPU’s features and code libraries work well with these popular AI development tools, just as the original PyTorch does. Plus the search giant has launched a dedicated tool, the TPU agent suite , to help developers move their apps to Google’s chips and cloud and fix errors along the way. It even updated its popular LiteRT tool, which runs AI on phones, laptops and embedded devices, to work better with PyTorch AI apps. None of this means AI app developers will automatically ditch Nvidia’s hardware en masse just because they can now easily move to alternative chips and clouds. But Amazon and Google are clearly working to end Nvidia’s advantage.

item.title: MPS in PyTorch 2.15
item.abstract:
Back to Articles MPS in PyTorch 2.15 Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 8 +2 Irakli Salia Isalia20 Follow Khushi Agrawal khushi-411 Follow If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads. A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors. TL;DR FP8 comes to the Mac: store float8_e4m3fn values in half the space of BF16 and use scaled matrix multiplication and all other ops which are supported on CUDA/CPU! MoE models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s on an M3 Ultra, thanks to a native grouped matmul with a dedicated decoding path, fewer GPU-CPU syncs and faster top-k routing. Less time per token for every LLM: single-row linear layers use specialized matrix-vector kernels, and softmax over the vocabulary is about 8× faster. More linear algebra on the GPU: complex LU and triangular solves, faster small-matrix inverses, and faster QR decomposition. Audio, video, and training get attention too: faster paths for convolutions, padding, dropout, interpolation backward and reductions. Wan2.2's video VAE decode now peaks at 8 GiB of memory instead of 270 GiB. More control from Python: public MPS streams and more reliable event timing. Updated requirements: MPS now requires macOS 15 or later ; PyTorch 2.15 requires Python 3.11 or later . A peek at 2.16: attention fully on Metal, more MPSGraph-to-Metal migrations and faster LLM decoding. What this means for you If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice: Much faster local LLMs. Mixture-of-experts models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: on an M3 Ultra with torch.compile , Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s and LFM2.5-8B-A1B from 23.6 to 123.6 tokens/s. Dense models benefit too, from faster linear layers and an 8× faster softmax for sampling. ( More ) Video generation that fits in memory. Decoding a video with Wan2.2's tiled VAE used to push driver memory to 270 GiB; it now peaks at about 8 GiB. ( More ) Correct image editing with Qwen-Image-2.1. On 2.14, the Qwen-Image-2.1 VAE encoder silently corrupted images on MPS, breaking image-edit workflows ( reported in ComfyUI ). The same padding change fixes it: an encode-decode round trip now matches CPU at 29.95 dB PSNR, up from 10.06 dB. FP8 weights on your Mac. FP8 tensors take half the memory of BF16, and F.scaled_mm multiplies them directly on the GPU. ( More ) Contents Getting started FP8 comes to MPS Faster language-model decoding Linear algebra gets a boost Convolutions, padding, and training Softmax and reductions A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding More control with MPS streams More operations work on MPS A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16 Wrapping up Getting started You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix ). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why. To try the release candidate in a separate environment: uv pip install torch==2.15.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu FP8 comes to MPS FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16. You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm , which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor: import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def quantize_fp8 ( x ): limit = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn). max scale = x. abs ().amax().clamp_min( 1e-12 ) / limit return (x / scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn), scale x = torch.randn( 1 , 1024 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.float32)
weight = torch.randn( 1024 , 1024 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.float32)
x_fp8, x_scale = quantize_fp8(x)
w_fp8, w_scale = quantize_fp8(weight) y = F.scaled_mm( x_fp8, w_fp8.t(), scale_a=x_scale, scale_recipe_a=F.ScalingType.TensorWise, scale_b=w_scale, scale_recipe_b=F.ScalingType.TensorWise, output_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
) print (y.shape, y.dtype) Faster language-model decoding Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers. Linear layers MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear , so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup . The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×. Mixture-of-experts layers A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation . In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well. For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16: import torch import torch.nn.functional as F tokens = torch.randn( 64 , 64 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.bfloat16)
weights = torch.randn( 3 , 128 , 64 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.bfloat16)
ends = torch.tensor([ 16 , 48 , 64 ], device= "mps" , dtype=torch.int32) out = F.grouped_mm(tokens, weights.transpose(- 2 , - 1 ), offs=ends) print (out.shape) # torch.Size([64, 128]) The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile , MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second : Linear algebra gets a boost Complex-valued computations Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization , LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU: import torch a = torch.randn( 8 , 8 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.complex64)
a = a + 8 * torch.eye( 8 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.complex64)
b = torch.randn( 8 , 2 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.complex64) lu, pivots = torch.linalg.lu_factor(a)
x = torch.linalg.lu_solve(lu, pivots, b) print ((a @ x - b). abs (). max ().item()) Small matrices and larger solves Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving.

item.title: Cloudflare Releases Clairic, a System One Extraction Model on Workers AI
item.abstract: Cloudflare has released a preview of Clairic , a new System One extraction model on Workers AI. The Cloudflare Clairic extraction model reads text or images and returns typed values, not generated text. It targets a job developers usually give to LLMs: pulling totals, dates and IDs into JSON. Clairic answers every requested field in 1 forward pass, with no reasoning and no output tokens. Clairic is a Cloudflare model that extracts, computes, estimates and forecasts typed values from unstructured inputs. It builds on the System One idea from TypeSafe’s Jev , named for Kahneman’s fast, intuitive thinking. Jev and Cloudflare’s own Clef are decision models. They score options you list in advance. Clairic covers answers you cannot list, such as an invoice total, a date or a repair cost. Cloudflare frames a 3-part stack. Extraction models turn raw input into typed values. Decision models turn values into decisions. LLMs turn decisions into words. A request has a state (text plus up to 4 images) and a map of named, typed fields . Each field can carry plain-language instructions. Supported types are text, number, date, time, datetime, duration, list, estimate and forecast, per the Workers AI changelog . Every scalar answer includes p_null , the probability that the value is absent, plus a confidence score. Text answers return exact spans with character offsets. Estimates and forecasts return a median and an 80% interval, from p10 to p90. Forecasts cover up to 64 steps. There is no field limit. Fields that do not fit beside the input in one 8,192-token pass split into parallel passes. Each pass sees the whole input. In the docs example, a 61-token invoice ran in 3 passes. It billed 655 input tokens, including 472 schema tokens. Wide schemas can cost more than the document itself. In a support-email example, Clairic added price and tax into $701.10. It also computed 11 days since delivery. Neither number appears in the email. A missing tracking number returned null instead of a plausible guess. On a skewed receipt photo, it read all 7 present values and returned null for the absent discount. Its lowest confidence was 0.776, on the order number. For forecasting, Cloudflare predicted daily TSA checkpoint counts for 21 days. Average error was 3.3%. 17 of 21 actual counts fell inside the 80% interval. 3 of the 4 misses fell on Columbus Day weekend. The main test is a damaged-product claims pipeline. Clairic extracted facts, Clef chose refund or repair, and GLM-5.3 wrote the reply. Cloudflare compared this against GLM-5.3 handling all 3 steps. The cascade finished in 19.3 s versus 61.7 s, about 3.2x faster. Extraction took 0.46 s against 16.1 s. The decision step took 0.22 s against 21.9 s. Cost per million claims fell 49%, from $11,740 to $6,032. The reply step still dominated, at 18.6 of the 19.3 s. Both pipelines got the facts and decision right. Clairic’s repair estimate was identical across runs. GLM-5.3 returned $250, $250 and $220. Cloudflare says Gemma 4 and Qwen failed the all-LLM version. Clairic is live as a preview at @cf/cloudflare/clairic . Call it through the Workers AI binding with env.AI.run() or the REST API. AI Gateway works with the same endpoints. Pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens with no output charge. That undercuts Clef’s $0.24 but sits above Jev’s $0.042. Weights are promised but not yet released. Check out the Cloudflare blog post , the Clairic model docs , the extraction models explainer and the Workers AI changelog . Also read our earlier coverage of Drex 1.5 . item.title: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as ‘frontier models can’t be trusted’
item.abstract: Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents. The launch comes as Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents. Perhaps the most notable addition is Guardian Agents , a new feature intended to monitor the AI agents a company uses. Guardian Agents is part of Project Perception, a product introduced in June. Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak. Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them. The product was designed around the assumption that AI hackers would come from outside the company. But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.” Earlier this month, in his private blog , Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products. He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch. “We are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data and giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!” he wrote. “We simply can’t outsource responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf. A model provider’s assurances do not relieve us of that responsibility. … In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.” When announcing Guardian Agents, Microsoft’s security business chief Hayete Gallot was even more straightforward. “Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote , adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable. They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.” On top of that, they are often given the keys to the kingdom, with access to data and tools that could do serious harm. Microsoft’s solution is both surprising and self-serving. The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both. OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models. So, Microsoft is sowing distrust against some of its own business interests. The self-serving side is that Microsoft wants enterprises to buy agent security products from it, the cloud provider, rather than from Anthropic and OpenAI. But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound. The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit. Or as Nadella puts it: “We need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.” Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways. In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw. It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task. That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions. This idea of agents as untrustworthy insiders is taking hold across the broader industry, too. Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies . The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch. This follows Microsoft’s announcement of the new Surface Laptop Ultra PCs built for agents , which run on Nvidia chips and have agent security and controls baked in.

item.title: AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms
item.abstract:
Back to Articles AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 3 Mattt mattt Follow Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog:
a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework
that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses.
We heard from app developers who were curious about local models
but weren't always sure how to get started.
They also wanted to avoid the added complexity
of supporting multiple inference providers.
AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback. Local and hosted inference each have their strengths,
and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps.
A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task. A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out,
along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0 . Here's what changed, and what's next: A drop-in compatible API The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same:
use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app.
To get started, change your import statement: - import FoundationModels + import AnyLanguageModel The same session code then works with the system model,
with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML,
and with the hosted providers below. Over the past year, we've added several major features: Tool calling works with every provider. Guided generation works with every provider, too,
including nested @Generable types and arrays of them. Image support lets you attach images to prompts
using Foundation Models 27's syntax,
including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27. On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with
any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol,
including Core AI models. Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps. Hosted models, too Support for hosted models expanded this year, too.
AnyLanguageModel now supports: OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs Open Responses ,
for any provider with a compatible endpoint Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options Google's Gemini API Ollama Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27 Hugging Face Inference Providers ,
and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter,
through a custom base URL With Inference Providers,
you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device
with the same session code: let model = OpenAILanguageModel ( baseURL: URL (string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/" ) ! , apiKey: ProcessInfo .processInfo.environment[ "HF_TOKEN" ] ! , model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b" , apiVariant: .chatCompletions
) Hosted providers get the same features as local models:
guided generation, tool calling with streaming,
and token usage on responses. Reasoning is now part of the transcript too.
When you switch providers,
reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them. API keys come from a closure instead of a string,
so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server.
The README explains when to let people bring their own keys
and when to route requests through a proxy. AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux,
so the same code can work on a server. Open-weight models got better While we've made local models easier to use,
the models themselves have become more capable,
making the small ones a good place to start.
Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now: Gemma 4 E2B from Google,
in GGUF, about 3.4 GB at Q4_0 with quantization-aware training. LFM2.5 2.6B from Liquid AI,
in GGUF, about 1.7 GB at Q4_K_M . Qwen3.8 27B for MLX from Alibaba,
about 16 GB at 4 bits. The first two fit on an iPhone,
and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more.
Selecting the MLX model takes one line: let model = MLXLanguageModel (modelId: "mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit" ) And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16.
For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers. Upgrading to 1.0 dependencies: [ .package( url: "https://github.com/huggingface/AnyLanguageModel" , from: "1.0.0" , traits: [ "MLX" ] )
] If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel , swift-huggingface ,
and swift-xet release notes
for help updating your code. Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features.
Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers. What's next Language models have proven to be a powerful tool
for building intelligence into products.
They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work.
We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities:
familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device.
Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen. Links AnyLanguageModel on GitHub swift-huggingface on GitHub swift-xet on GitHub Introducing AnyLanguageModel Introducing swift-huggingface
